newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG defence chief says unaware of mercenary plan.
newsitem.headline: PNG defence chief says unaware of mercenary plan.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's defence chief on Monday denied reports his government planned to use mercenaries against secessionist rebels on Bougainville, calling recent troop movements part of ongoing training.
"We are currently doing some level of training and are involving a number of countries' specialist forces," said Defence Force Chief-of-Staff Colonel Jack Tuat.

"We are occasionally bringing in people to train our guys on the use of new and specific equipment," Tuat told Reuters. "The training is part of capacity building by the defence forces to be able to contain any security problem."
Tuat said the training involved Australia, New Zealand and the United States, but refused to identify who was taking part or whether it included non-government soldiers.

Australian newspapers have said the South Pacific nation planned to bring in up to 150 Africa-based mercenaries for an operation to capture or kill the leaders of the pro-independence Bougainville Revolutionary Army.
They said the government had approved a A$36-million (US$27-million) covert operation to end the nine-year rebellion on Bougainville, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.
"I do not know what they are talking about," said Tuat.
Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan has refused to confirm or deny the reports about the mercenaries.
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said on Monday he had warned Chan not to use mercenaries against the rebels on Bougainville.
Downer said he told Chan during a visit to Port Moresby last week that this would significantly damage the country's international standing.
"It's a matter of profound concern to the (Australian) federal government that this is happening," Downer told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio.

"What I made clear to Sir Julius Chan and to other ministers...was that if there was a resumption of any military activity on Bougainville, then it would be regarded by Australia as absolutely disastrous," Downer said.
"I will use any vehicle which is reasonable that I possibly can to try to stop this operation going ahead, but of course I don't wish to act outside the law myself," he said.

The Australian newspaper reported that military cargo aircraft leased to Sandlines International, a subsidiary of the British-registered company Executive Outcomes, had been flying in and out of Jackson Airport in Port Moresby last week.
Executive Outcomes is Africa's best known private army and has helped Angola and Sierra Leone fight rebel threats.

The Australian said the mercenaries would stage a "surgical strike" targetting hardline rebel leaders on Bougainville, while a second operation by mercenaries would try to free five Papua New Guinea soldiers held captive by rebels.
In Canberra, Australian Prime Minister John Howard told parliament that Australians in Bougainville had been warned of increasing danger after reports of mercenary involvement.
Hundreds of people have died from the fighting or disease due to a lack of medical supplies in the Bougainville rebellion.
